lesson.title: Particles, states and heat
points: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space, and it is made of very tiny particles.
The particles have gaps between them, keep moving all the time, and attract each other.
In a solid the particles are packed tightly and only vibrate; in a liquid they slide past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move freely.
Temperature in kelvin is K = °C + 273. Ice melts at 273 K (0°C) and water boils at 373 K (100°C), and the temperature stays fixed while the state changes.
lesson.story: When you stir sugar into nimbu pani, the sugar seems to vanish but the drink turns sweet. The sugar particles have spread into the gaps between the water particles.

example.q: Convert 27°C to kelvin and say in which state water is at that temperature.
steps: Water melts at 273 K and boils at 373 K. Since 300 K lies between these, water is a liquid.

questions.q: Which statement about the particles of matter is correct?
questions.why: Particles of matter attract each other. This force is strongest in solids and weakest in gases.

o.t: Particles of a solid are completely at rest
o.m: Believed solid particles do not move at all, instead of vibrating about fixed positions

o.t: There is no space between particles of a solid
o.m: Thought a solid is packed with no gaps because it feels hard

o.t: Particles of a liquid are fixed in one place
o.m: Mixed up liquids with solids and ignored that liquid particles slide past each other

questions.q: What is 100°C in kelvin?

o.m: Used the offset 273 as the answer and forgot to add the Celsius reading
Thought kelvin and Celsius readings are the same number
Subtracted 100 from 273 instead of adding

questions.q: An LPG gas cylinder can hold a large amount of gas squeezed into a small volume. Why can gases be compressed so easily?
questions.why: Gas particles are very far apart, so there is plenty of empty space that pressure can squeeze out.

o.t: The particles of gas themselves shrink under pressure
o.m: Thought the particles become smaller when compressed instead of moving closer together

o.t: There are large spaces between gas particles
Gas particles attract each other very strongly
o.m: Thought strong attraction makes a gas easy to squeeze; actually it is weakest in gases

o.t: Gas particles are at rest and can be packed together
o.m: Thought gas particles do not move, so they can be stacked like solids

questions.q: Ice at 0°C is heated and starts to melt. The thermometer reading stays at 0°C until all the ice melts. Where does the heat go?
questions.why: The heat (latent heat of fusion) is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles, so the state changes without a rise in temperature.

o.t: It is used to raise the temperature of the ice
o.m: Thought heat always raises the temperature, even during a change of state

o.t: It is lost to the surroundings and wasted
o.m: Thought the thermometer does not rise because the heat escapes

o.t: It makes each particle of ice grow bigger
o.m: Thought heat expands the particles themselves instead of loosening the attraction between them

o.t: It breaks the forces holding the particles together

questions.q: On a very humid day, wet clothes dry slowly. What is the reason?
questions.why: Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour, so less extra water can evaporate into it and the rate of evaporation decreases.

o.t: The air already has a lot of water vapour, so evaporation is slower
Evaporation stops completely when the air is humid
o.m: Thought evaporation must stop completely rather than slow down

o.t: Water becomes heavier in humid weather
o.m: Thought humidity changes the water in the clothes instead of the surrounding air

o.t: Humid air is always colder than dry air
o.m: Assumed humid air must be colder, which would make clothes dry slower, instead of linking it to vapour already in the air

questions.q: Water kept in a matka (earthen pot) stays cool in summer. What is the reason?
questions.why: Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates. Evaporation takes latent heat from the water inside, which cools it.

o.t: The clay absorbs all the heat and stores it
o.m: Thought the clay simply soaks up heat, ignoring that evaporation cools

o.t: Cold air from the surroundings enters the pot through the pores
o.m: Thought cool air flows into the pot instead of heat leaving by evaporation

o.t: Water evaporating from the pores takes heat from the water inside
The pot makes the water particles move faster so they feel cold

questions.q: Water at 0°C and ice at 0°C are both taken in the same mass. Which statement is correct?
questions.why: Water at 0°C has absorbed the latent heat of fusion, so it has more energy than ice at the same temperature.

o.t: Both have the same energy because the temperature is the same
o.m: Thought equal temperature means equal energy and ignored the heat absorbed during melting

o.t: Water at 0°C has more energy because it has absorbed latent heat
Ice has more energy because it is solid and compact

o.m: Thought the comparison is impossible without a temperature difference

questions.q: Camphor is heated in a china dish covered with an inverted funnel. After some time, a white solid collects on the inner walls of the funnel. Which changes took place?
questions.why: Camphor sublimes (solid to gas) and the vapour cools on the funnel wall and turns back directly into a solid.

lesson.title: Counting the tiny particles
points: Lavoisier's law of conservation of mass says mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Proust's law of constant proportions says a compound always has its elements in a fixed mass ratio, for example hydrogen to oxygen in water is 1 : 8.
An atom is the smallest particle of an element; a molecule is a group of atoms joined together, such as O₂ (two atoms) or O₃ (three atoms).
Atomic masses are measured in u (H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Na = 23, Cl = 35.5). The molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses in the formula.
One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles. The mass of one mole in grams equals the atomic or molecular mass, so moles = given mass ÷ molar mass.
lesson.story: A shopkeeper sells eggs by the dozen and not one by one. Chemists do the same with a mole, which is a fixed 'packet' of 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

example.q: How many moles are there in 22 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂? (C = 12 u, O = 16 u)
steps: So there are 0.5 mole of CO₂.

questions.q: Which scientist stated the law of conservation of mass?
questions.why: Antoine Lavoisier showed that the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.

o.m: Confused the law with Dalton's atomic theory, which explained it
Confused it with Proust's law of constant proportions
Linked the name with the mole and Avogadro's number instead of this law

questions.q: How many atoms are there in one molecule of ozone, O₃?
questions.why: The subscript 3 shows that one ozone molecule has three oxygen atoms, so its atomicity is 3.

o.m: Confused ozone with ordinary oxygen, O₂
Thought ozone is a single-atom (monoatomic) species
Confused ozone with phosphorus, P₄

questions.q: What is the molecular mass of water, H₂O? (H = 1 u, O = 16 u)
questions.why: Molecular mass = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 u.

o.m: Added 1 + 16 and ignored the subscript 2 on hydrogen
Swapped the subscripts and calculated as H₁O₂ = 1 + 32
Added the atomic numbers (1 + 1 + 8) instead of the atomic masses

questions.q: How many moles of water are there in 36 g of water? (Molar mass of water = 18 g)
questions.why: Moles = given mass ÷ molar mass = 36 ÷ 18 = 2 moles.

o.m: Inverted the formula and divided molar mass by the given mass

questions.q: Magnesium has valency 2 and chlorine has valency 1. What is the formula of magnesium chloride?
questions.why: Criss-crossing the valencies gives Mg₁Cl₂, which is written MgCl₂.

questions.q: How many atoms are present in 0.5 mole of oxygen gas, O₂? (Avogadro number = 6.022 × 10²³)
questions.why: 0.5 mole of O₂ has 3.011 × 10²³ molecules, and each molecule has 2 atoms, giving 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.

Doubled for the two atoms but ignored the 0.5 mole
Divided the Avogadro number by 10 instead of using 0.5 and 2 correctly

questions.q: In water, hydrogen and oxygen are always present in a mass ratio of 1 : 8. How much hydrogen is there in 9 g of water?
questions.why: The 9 parts of water split as 1 part hydrogen and 8 parts oxygen, so 9 g of water has 1 g of hydrogen.

o.m: Took the oxygen share as the hydrogen share
Assumed hydrogen and oxygen are present in equal amounts
Used the number of hydrogen atoms (2) as its mass

questions.q: 10 g of calcium carbonate is strongly heated in a closed container. It gives 5.6 g of calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas. What is the mass of carbon dioxide formed?
questions.why: By conservation of mass, total mass of products = 10 g, so carbon dioxide = 10 − 5.6 = 4.4 g.

o.m: Assumed both products have the same mass
Added the two given masses instead of subtracting
Thought each product separately must equal the mass of the reactant

lesson.title: The cell and its parts
points: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Robert Hooke first saw cells in a slice of cork in 1665.
Cells without a true nucleus (nuclear membrane) are prokaryotic, like bacteria. Cells with a membrane-bound nucleus are eukaryotic.

Organelles do different jobs: mitochondria release energy, the Golgi apparatus packages materials, ribosomes make proteins, lysosomes digest waste, and plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
The plasma membrane is selectively permeable. Water moves through it by osmosis, from higher water concentration to lower water concentration.
lesson.story: A cell is like a tiny kirana shop: the shutter lets only some things in and out, the counter packs goods, and the generator in the back gives power to everything.

example.q: A plant cell is placed in a strong salt solution. What happens to it?
steps: The salt solution has less free water than the cell sap, so it is hypertonic.
Water moves out of the cell through the plasma membrane by osmosis.
The cell contents shrink and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall (plasmolysis).

questions.q: Who first observed cells in a thin slice of cork?
questions.why: Robert Hooke observed the box-like compartments in cork in 1665 and named them cells.

o.m: Confused him with the discoverer of the nucleus
Confused cork cells with the living cells Leeuwenhoek first saw in pond water

questions.q: Which cell organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.why: Mitochondria release energy from food as ATP, so they are called the powerhouse of the cell.

Confused waste disposal with energy production

questions.q: Which structure is present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell?
questions.why: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the plasma membrane. Animal cells do not.

o.m: Thought only plant cells have a boundary layer, though every cell has a plasma membrane

questions.q: Which feature do bacterial cells lack?
questions.why: Bacteria are prokaryotes. Their genetic material lies in a nucleoid without a nuclear membrane.

questions.q: A plant cell is kept in a very concentrated sugar solution. What happens?
questions.why: The solution outside has less free water, so water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell shrinks.

o.m: Reversed the direction of osmosis

questions.q: A chemical stops the lysosomes of a cell from working. What is most likely to build up inside the cell?
questions.why: Lysosomes digest foreign material and worn-out organelles, so these would pile up if lysosomes failed.

o.m: Confused lysosomes with ribosomes, which make proteins
Confused lysosomes with mitochondria, which release energy

questions.q: Dry raisins are soaked in water and swell up after some time. What is the reason?
questions.why: Raisins have a lower water concentration than the water outside, so water enters through their membranes by osmosis.

o.t: The cell wall of the raisin pumps in water using energy

o.t: Sugar moves out of the raisins and leaves space for air

o.t: The raisins absorb water vapour from the air only
o.m: Ignored osmosis and thought only vapour from air is involved

questions.q: A cell makes a protein and sends it out. In which order do the organelles take part?
questions.why: Ribosomes on the rough ER make the protein, and the Golgi apparatus then packages and sends it out.

o.m: Reversed the order and thought packaging comes before the protein is made

lesson.title: Describing motion
points: Distance is the total path length and is a scalar. Displacement is the shortest straight-line change in position and is a vector, so it can even be zero.
Speed = distance ÷ time, and velocity = displacement ÷ time. Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time, a = (v − u) ÷ t, measured in m/s².
The three equations for uniform acceleration are v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as.
Motion in a circle at constant speed is accelerated motion because the direction, and so the velocity, keeps changing.
lesson.story: A cricketer runs one full lap of the ground and stops where he started. His odometer-like distance is big, yet his displacement is zero.

example.q: A car starts from rest and moves with an acceleration of 2 m/s² for 5 s. Find its final velocity and the distance covered.
steps: u = 0, a = 2 m/s², t = 5 s. Use v = u + at: v = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 m/s.
Use s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 2 × 5² = 25 m.
The car reaches 10 m/s and covers 25 m.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of velocity?
questions.why: Velocity is displacement per unit time, so its SI unit is metre per second (m/s).

o.m: Gave the unit of acceleration
Used an everyday unit that is not the SI unit
Gave the unit of displacement and left out the time

questions.q: Which one of these quantities is a vector?
questions.why: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Distance, speed and time are scalars.

o.m: Thought distance has a direction because it is measured along a path
Thought speed has a direction because a vehicle moves in one
Thought any measured quantity that changes is a vector

questions.q: A bus covers 180 km in 4 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.why: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 180 ÷ 4 = 45 km/h.

o.m: Multiplied distance by time instead of dividing
Subtracted the time from the distance
Divided the distance by 2 instead of by the time

questions.q: A scooter speeds up from 10 m/s to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?

o.m: Divided the final velocity alone by the time instead of the change in velocity
Added the two velocities instead of subtracting them
Divided time by the change in velocity, inverting the formula

questions.q: An athlete runs exactly one full lap of a 400 m circular track and stops at the starting point. What is the displacement?
questions.why: Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to end. Start and end are the same point, so it is zero.

o.m: Treated displacement as the same as the distance travelled
Took the straight-line distance across the track instead of between start and end
Doubled the distance by counting the return as well

questions.q: A train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.5 m/s² for 20 s. How far does it travel?

o.m: Left out the ½ in the equation
Gave the final velocity (0.5 × 20) as the distance
Used ½at without squaring the time

questions.q: A car moving at 20 m/s is braked and slows down uniformly at 5 m/s² until it stops. What distance does it cover while stopping?
questions.why: Using v² = u² + 2as with v = 0: 0 = 400 − 2 × 5 × s, so s = 40 m.

o.m: Used u² ÷ a and left out the factor 2 in 2as
Calculated the stopping time (u ÷ a) and gave it as the distance
Multiplied the speed by the retardation

questions.q: A car moves around a circular road at a constant speed of 60 km/h. Which statement is correct?
questions.why: The direction changes at every instant, so the velocity changes. A changing velocity means the motion is accelerated even though the speed is constant.

o.t: Its velocity keeps changing, so it is accelerating
Its velocity is constant because the speed is constant
o.m: Treated speed and velocity as the same and ignored the change of direction

o.t: Its acceleration is zero because it does not speed up

o.t: Its displacement always equals the distance it travels

lesson.title: Newton's three laws
points: First law: a body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless an unbalanced force acts on it. This tendency is inertia, and a heavier body has more inertia.
Momentum is p = mv. Second law: the force is the rate of change of momentum, and for a constant mass F = ma. One newton is 1 kg m/s².
Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The two forces act on two different bodies.
When bodies interact, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after (conservation of momentum), as in the recoil of a gun.
lesson.story: When a bus brakes suddenly, you lurch forward. The bus stops but your body wants to keep moving, which is inertia.

example.q: A force acts on a 1000 kg car and gives it an acceleration of 3 m/s². Find the force.

questions.q: What is the name of the property of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or motion?
questions.why: This property is called inertia, and it depends on the mass of the body.

o.m: Confused resisting a change with the quantity of motion (mass × velocity)
Confused resistance to change with the rate of change of velocity
Thought that only friction resists a change in motion

questions.q: Which of these is the SI unit of force?
questions.why: The SI unit of force is the newton (N), equal to 1 kg m/s².

o.m: Gave the unit of momentum
Gave the unit of work and energy
Gave the unit of mass instead of force

questions.q: What force is needed to give a 5 kg trolley an acceleration of 3 m/s²?

o.m: Added the mass and the acceleration
Divided mass by acceleration
Divided acceleration by mass

questions.q: When a bus suddenly brakes, the passengers jerk forward. What is the reason?
questions.why: The passengers' bodies tend to keep moving forward in their state of motion (inertia) while the bus slows down.

o.t: The brakes push the passengers forward
o.m: Thought a forward force acts on the passengers when the brakes are applied

o.t: Their bodies tend to continue moving forward due to inertia

o.m: Thought gravity acts horizontally in the direction of the bus

o.t: The mass of the passengers increases when the bus stops
o.m: Thought that braking changes the mass of the passengers

questions.why: By the third law the bullet exerts an equal and opposite force on the gun, which pushes the gun backwards.

o.t: The reaction force is smaller because the gun is heavier
o.m: Thought the reaction force depends on the mass and is not equal to the action

o.t: Air resistance pushes the gun backwards
o.m: Thought a push from the air and not the bullet causes the recoil

o.m: Used the final velocity alone (20 ÷ 5) as the acceleration
Added the two velocities instead of subtracting them

questions.why: Momentum is conserved: 0.02 × 100 = 4 × v, so v = 0.5 m/s (backwards).

o.m: Used 20 g without converting to kilograms

questions.why: The ball's momentum change is fixed, so increasing the time of stopping reduces the force (F = change in momentum ÷ time).

o.t: It reduces the momentum that the ball originally had

lesson.title: Gravity, work and energy
points: Newton's law of gravitation: every two bodies attract each other with a force F = G m₁m₂ ÷ d². Force grows with the masses and falls with the square of the distance. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg².
Near the Earth all freely falling bodies have the same acceleration g = 9.8 m/s². Mass stays the same everywhere, but weight (mg) on the Moon is about one-sixth of that on Earth.
Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs, in joules. Kinetic energy is ½mv², potential energy is mgh, and energy changes form without being lost.
Power is the rate of doing work, P = W ÷ t, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).
lesson.story: A coconut falling from a tree gains speed as it drops. Its stored energy mgh at the top turns into movement energy ½mv² near the ground.

example.q: A boy lifts a 5 kg bag through 2 m. Find the work done against gravity. (g = 10 m/s²)
steps: The force needed equals the weight: F = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N.
Displacement s = 2 m in the direction of the force.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of work?
questions.why: Work = force × displacement, and its SI unit is the joule (J).

o.m: Confused work with power, which is measured in watts
Gave the unit of the force instead of the work
Gave the unit of pressure

questions.q: What is the value of acceleration due to gravity (g) near the Earth's surface?
questions.why: Near the Earth's surface g is about 9.8 m/s².

o.m: Gave the value of the universal gravitational constant G instead
Gave the approximate value for the Moon
Placed the decimal point wrongly

questions.q: What is the potential energy of a 10 kg object kept at a height of 5 m? (g = 10 m/s²)

questions.why: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J.

questions.q: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. What are his mass and weight on the Moon?
questions.why: Mass does not change with place, but weight is mg and g on the Moon is about one-sixth of that on Earth, so his weight is about one-sixth.

o.t: Mass stays 60 kg and weight is about one-sixth of that on Earth
Mass becomes 10 kg and weight is one-sixth of that on Earth
o.m: Thought mass also reduces on the Moon, mixing up mass and weight

o.m: Thought weight does not change with place, ignoring the change in g

questions.q: Two bodies attract each other with a gravitational force F. If both masses are doubled and the distance between them is also doubled, what is the new force?
questions.why: F is proportional to m₁m₂ ÷ d². The numerator becomes 4 times and d² also becomes 4 times, so F is unchanged.

o.m: Doubled both masses but ignored the change in distance
Applied the doubling of distance only and ignored the doubled masses
Treated the force as depending on only one mass doubling

questions.q: A pump lifts 100 kg of water to a height of 10 m in 20 s. What is the power of the pump? (g = 10 m/s²)

o.m: Gave the work done as the power and did not divide by time
Forgot g while calculating the work
Divided only the mass by the time

questions.q: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower and reaches the ground in 3 s. How high is the tower? (g = 10 m/s², initial velocity = 0)
questions.why: s = ut + ½gt² = 0 + ½ × 10 × 3² = 45 m.

lesson.title: How sound travels
points: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and travels as a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions. It needs a material medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases, and it moves faster when the temperature rises.
Frequency (Hz) decides the pitch, and amplitude decides the loudness. The wave speed is v = f × λ. Humans hear from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; below this is infrasound and above it is ultrasound.
An echo is the reflection of sound, and the sound must travel to the obstacle and back, so the time is t = 2d ÷ v. SONAR uses ultrasound to measure the depth of the sea.
lesson.story: When you shout towards the walls of an empty hall at your school, your own voice comes back after a short gap. That is an echo, sound bouncing back from the wall.

example.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 200 Hz and a wavelength of 1.7 m. Find its speed.

questions.q: What type of wave is a sound wave in air?
questions.why: Particles of air vibrate back and forth along the direction in which the wave moves, so sound in air is a longitudinal wave.

o.m: Thought sound is like ripples on water or waves on a rope
Thought sound behaves like light and does not need a medium
Thought air carries both kinds of wave like solids may

questions.q: Through which of these can sound NOT travel?
questions.why: Sound needs a medium made of particles, so it cannot travel through a vacuum.

o.m: Believed sound only travels in air and not in liquids
Believed solids block sound

o.t: Air with some dust in it
o.m: Thought the presence of dust or impurities would stop sound

questions.q: A source vibrates at 200 Hz and produces waves of wavelength 1.7 m. What is the speed of the wave?

o.m: Divided the frequency by the wavelength
Added the frequency and the wavelength
Divided the wavelength by the frequency

questions.q: A guitar string is plucked harder. Which property of the sound increases?
questions.why: A harder pluck gives the string a larger amplitude, which makes the sound louder. The frequency (pitch) does not change.

o.m: Confused loudness with pitch
Thought a larger vibration also means more vibrations per second
Thought a stronger source makes sound travel faster

questions.q: If you put your ear on a railway track, you can hear an approaching train before you hear it through the air. Why?
questions.why: Sound travels faster in a solid like steel than in air, so it reaches your ear sooner through the track.

o.t: Sound travels faster in steel than in air
Sound travels faster in air than in steel
o.m: Thought sound is faster in gases than in solids

o.t: The steel track makes the sound louder, so it is heard earlier
o.m: Mixed up loudness with speed of the sound

o.t: Sound travels at the same speed in steel and in air
o.m: Thought the speed does not depend on the medium

questions.q: A girl claps near a wall that is 85 m away. After how much time will she hear the echo? (speed of sound in air = 340 m/s)
questions.why: The sound travels 2 × 85 = 170 m to the wall and back. Time = 170 ÷ 340 = 0.5 s.

o.m: Used only the one-way distance and forgot the return trip
Divided the speed by the distance, inverting the formula

questions.q: A ship sends an ultrasound pulse down and receives the echo from the sea bed after 4 s. If the speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s, what is the depth of the sea?
questions.why: The pulse goes down and back, so depth = (1500 × 4) ÷ 2 = 3000 m.

o.m: Used the full time as if the pulse went one way only
Divided the speed by the time

questions.q: A source produces sound of frequency 15 Hz and another produces 30 kHz. Which statement is correct for a normal human ear?
questions.why: The audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz. 15 Hz is infrasound and 30 kHz is ultrasound, so neither can be heard.

o.m: Thought all vibrating sources can be heard by a human ear

o.t: Only 30 kHz can be heard because it has a higher frequency
o.m: Thought the higher the frequency, the more audible the sound
